videos.description:
Bankulli sits down with Trending for a wide-ranging conversation on the Nigerian music industry, The Headies, the Grammys, respect, and his new project, Chronicles of Afrobeats.

In the conversation, Bankulli shares his thoughts on why “Grammy is an American award, not a Nigerian award” and why he believes Nigerians should pay more attention to The Headies and what the award represents for the Nigerian music industry.

He also speaks on the importance of respect within the music industry, emphasizing that respect is reciprocal, while reflecting on the recognition artists receive from major award platforms.

Bankulli also discusses Chronicles of Afrobeats and the importance of documenting and preserving the story of Afrobeats.

He weighs in on the criticism surrounding The Headies, urging people not to be too harsh on the awards, especially considering that The Headies is only about 20 years old, while the Grammys has been around for over 60 years.

From Ayra Starr and Wizkid to the evolution of Afrobeats and the future of Nigerian music, Bankulli gives his perspective on the industry and the people shaping it.

Watch the full conversation and let us know what you think.

videos.headline: I Recovered Nearly ₦100M in Unclaimed Music Royalties for an OG | Treasure Mose on Music Rights
videos.description:
How much money could Nigerian artists be leaving unclaimed?

On this episode of Hits Don't Lie, Mannie Essien sits down with entertainment lawyer  Treasure Mose for a deep dive into the business and legal side of Nigerian music — from music royalties and publishing to masters, contracts, record labels and artists’ rights**.

Treasure shares one of the most shocking cases she handled involving an OG artist she grew up listening to, who had been performing hit songs without collecting the royalties attached to his music. She reveals how her team recovered close to ₦100 million in unclaimed royalties for an artist who didn’t know the money existed.

The conversation also breaks down:

• What music royalties actually are — beyond Spotify and Apple Music streams
• The difference between **streaming, publishing, distribution and synchronization royalties**
• How artists can find and claim unclaimed royalties
• Why having a hit song doesn't automatically mean you're getting paid
• What **masters** are and why ownership matters
• How record labels can own or control an artist's music
• Why artists should use **split sheets** when creating music with producers and songwriters
• Common mistakes artists make when signing record deals
• Automatic renewal clauses and other contract terms artists should understand
• Why artists need an **entertainment lawyer** before signing major agreements
• How artists can protect their names through **trademark registration**
• What happens when music rights become the subject of a legal dispute
• The difference between transferring music rights and selling a music catalogue
• Why artists should treat their careers like a business

This is a conversation about the part of the music industry that happens behind the music — and why understanding your rights can be just as important as making the hit.

**Watch the full episode and tell us your biggest takeaway in the comments.**

videos.title: "I'm Not A TikToker, I'm A Filmmaker" - Gilmore On Streaming, Creativity & His New Chapter
videos.headline: "I'm Not A TikToker, I'm A Filmmaker" - Gilmore On Streaming, Creativity & His New Chapter
videos.description:
Gilmore is leveling up. From TikTok to Twitch. From skits to streaming. And he is bringing the whole culture with him. In this exclusive interview, Gilmore opens up about his transition from short-form content to long-form streaming. He talks about why he is making the switch, what fans can expect, and who he looks up to in the streaming space.

He does not hold back on his favorite streamer. CarterEfe gets the crown. Spontaneous. Versatile. Creative. Painting rooms. Turning studios into beaches. Bringing camels and donkeys into a small space. Gilmore breaks down exactly why CarterEfe is the best in the game right now. And he gives Shank his flowers too. The blueprint is there. The global impact is real. But CarterEfe's consistency and creativity? Unmatched.

He also talks about Peller. Does his success come from being one of the best streamers or from his personality? Gilmore says Peller is super blessed and he is himself. That is the secret.

Gilmore also reveals his next big move. A six-day boarding school stream from the 23rd to the 29th. Costume days. Red nights. Cutting grass. Making Gary cake. Choco bonbon. It is back to back. And he is inviting everyone to tune in on Twitch. He talks about his goals. Slow and steady. Walk-ins. 9mm. No flying. Just climbing step by step. And he predicts a future where Nigerian streamers are on Lamborghinis. Where content creators and streamers become richer than musicians. This is the energy. This is the vision.

videos.headline: "You Have To Put Your Life In It" - Ladipoe Artistry, Talent & Why Artists Are Dodging Sacrifice
videos.description:
Ladipoe is not holding back. In this exclusive interview on the Morning Rush with Dreal Eve, he opens up about the real meaning behind "No Level" and why it should be the soundtrack to all your beefs. He talks about the people who pride themselves on being considerate and how sometimes you have to set boundaries. This song is for those who normally stay quiet. Now is your chance to speak up.

He also gets candid about the music industry and how things have changed. Discoverability is easier now with algorithms and platforms, but that does not mean talent is gone. It has just shifted to other places. He calls out lazy artists who are dodging the sacrifice it takes to be a real artist. For Ladipoe, you have to put your life in the music. That is what separates real artistry from just another income stream.

The conversation takes a personal turn when he talks about "Chosen" and the prayer his mother sent him. He cherished it for a long time and knew it had to be on that song. Where they are from, a mother's prayer is powerful. He also reveals his favorite songs on the album, including Palm Trees, Compose and Friend Indeed. And when asked who the hardest rapper in Nigeria is right now? His answer is simple. "Me. Period."

videos.description:
Abi and Araga are out of the Big Brother Nigeria house and they are holding nothing back. In this exclusive interview, they open up about their journey from the first night to the final weeks. Abi, the first female Head of House twice, talks about the weight of the crown and how she had to switch her leadership style to keep the house together. Araga opens up about finding his circle, the friendships that mattered, and the moments that tested him.

Then the conversation turns to Nomy. Her disqualification. Did she deserve it? Did they see it coming? Abi says she figured it was going to happen. Araga says her attitude made it obvious. But the real bombshell comes when they are asked about their relationship with Nomy outside the house. Abi says she cannot be friends with someone who ignored her during a task and disrespected the team. Araga says he was never friends with her and does not see that changing. The friendship question gets a hard no from both.

They also talk about who they want to keep in their lives. Gerard and Yusuf are definite for Araga. Cassie gets a mention from Abi but she thought it was fake. Chimsom chuka never aligned. The house was a confined space and most relationships were just for show. Real life is different.

And they reveal their plans after the house. Abi wants to go to pilot school and make enough money to sponsor herself. Araga is a fashion model, actor, entrepreneur and athlete. He runs 100 and 200 meters and dreams of representing Nigeria. He also has an eyewear line called Araga that he has been building for four years.

videos.title: How Salem King Became Nigeria's Ultimate Creator
videos.headline: How Salem King Became Nigeria's Ultimate Creator
videos.description:
​@salemkinging didn’t set out to become a full-time creator.

The son of ministers, Salem grew up in a home that encouraged curiosity, reading and asking questions. He went on to study Economics at university before entering the world of real estate, where he sold some of the most expensive properties in Nigeria’s most exclusive neighbourhoods.

Then, on the side, he started making content.

What began as a creative experiment quickly turned into something much bigger. His content found an audience, went viral and opened up opportunities he hadn't expected. As his platform grew, Salem began teaching others what he had learnt, sharing his knowledge through a series of classes designed to help aspiring creators build their confidence and find their voice.

Eventually, he made the decision to leave his job and pursue content creation full-time.

Today, Salem King is building the Creatorium franchise and positioning himself at the centre of Nigeria's rapidly evolving creator economy.

In this episode, we talk about his childhood, his journey from Economics to real estate, the moment he discovered the power of content, what going viral really changed, leaving a conventional career behind and what it takes to build a sustainable life as a creator.

videos.title: How Ladipoe Became One of Nigeria's Best Rappers
videos.headline: How Ladipoe Became One of Nigeria's Best Rappers
videos.description:
​@LadipoeLOTR  studied Biology and Chemistry at the University of North Carolina before moving back home to Nigeria, hoping to make the big break as a Recording Artist. 

He was in luck. His mother found a kindred spirit: another rapper’s mother while taking a course at the Lagos Business School. That rapper was Wale “Tec” Davies of @showdemcamp. Tec felt his bars and invited him into a creative circle, which incubated acts like Show Dem Camp, Funbi, @temidollfacevevo4701, @temsbaby, and more. 

Poe announced his presence on “Feel Alright”- a collab with SDC and @Bojdrb, which has been credited as being a precursor to the iconic Palm Wine Music series. 

Don Jazzy's @MavinRecords  came calling, and Poe vowed to make the best of the opportunity. Nearly 10 years later, he’s found the type of mainstream appeal that once seemed out of reach. This year, he released "Revival", one of the year’s best releases, highlighting why he’s one of the country’s most beloved artists.  

On this episode of Overnight Success, he takes us on the long journey from medical professional to one of the country's premier rappers.

videos.title: Maiya the Don Talks "Precious Cargo" & Shifting From Beauty Content to Music | The Almanac of Rap
videos.headline: Maiya the Don Talks "Precious Cargo" & Shifting From Beauty Content to Music | The Almanac of Rap
videos.description:
Maiya the Don spent three years figuring out what she actually wanted to say. After Hot Commodity introduced a Brooklyn rapper capable of moving between drill, pop and straight-up bars, touring with Flo Milli and building an audience that first knew her as a beauty creator, Maiya found herself confronting a harder question: what does her music sound like when she's no longer trying to prove she can do everything? 

On this episode of The Almanac of Rap, she talks to Donwill about creating The Fine Print Club, her book club built around reading, community and creating space for Black women; recommends everything from S.A. Cosby to DMX; and hilariously puts her literary knowledge to the test against some of urban fiction's wildest book titles. 

Between books and bars, she also makes a case for independence, explains why artists shouldn't run from being content creators and delivers a warning to anyone tempted to underestimate her pen: Precious Cargo (her new album) may be personal, but Maiya the Don still came to rap. Maiya the Don breaks down:

- Why Precious Cargo became the coming-of-age album she needed three years to make
- Turning a beauty-content following into the foundation for a rap career
- Why independence gives her control over both her artistry and narrative
- Building The Fine Print Club and creating literary community for Black women
- Why “TSA” is her answer to anyone questioning a woman rapper's pen
